articles.title: New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal links to extremists and Saudi state
articles.summary: The footage and other evidence the FBI failed to share undermine Omar al-Bayoumi's 25 years of denials.
articles.body:
The man at the heart of a $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought by 9/11 families had extensive links to Saudi government officials and went paintballing with one of al-Qaeda's future leaders, video obtained by the BBC reveals.

The footage, which the FBI had within days of the 2001 attacks, stands in stark contrast to Omar al-Bayoumi's 25 years of denials that he was an extremist and a Saudi spy.

Bayoumi, who claimed to be a student when he was in the United States, is seen in one clip embracing Anwar al-Awlaki, who would go on to lead al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. In another, Bayoumi and Awlaki are paintballing near San Diego with an official from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Islamic Affairs.

The videos form part of the 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia and have never been shown publicly before.

The lawsuit argues Saudi Arabia was complicit in the attacks and that Bayoumi aided two of the 19 hijackers who flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon - with another crashing in Pennsylvania.

Bayoumi was arrested in the UK by the Metropolitan Police days after the attacks and the videos were found among his possessions, along with other crucial evidence.

This included a diagram of a plane with a flight descent equation written alongside.

Multiple FBI agents received copies of the diagram, but it was never shared with the British interrogators, even though it had been couriered to the police station where Bayoumi was being held in custody.

The diagram was also kept from some FBI agents investigating Bayoumi, as well as from the 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the largest mass murder in US history, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed. Bayoumi was never prosecuted.

He and the Saudi government did not respond to the BBC's requests for comment, but both have always denied any involvement in, or prior knowledge of, the attacks. The FBI declined to comment.

After a judge ruled the lawsuit could go ahead in 2018, thousands of documents, as well as videos and photographs, have been released to the court and also declassified through an executive order made by former President Joe Biden.

BBC Panorama and Radio 4 have examined these documents, and spoken to dozens of special agents and investigators, to trace the evidence the FBI gathered about Bayoumi and Saudi Arabia's alleged involvement in 9/11 - and to understand why it was never fully pursued over 25 years.

The plane diagram was sent to the FBI's New York office and was analysed, according to an FBI source. But a US Department of Justice (DOJ) official told the BBC he was never shown a proposal to prosecute Bayoumi based on the evidence, even though "we've convicted people for less"

FBI agents in San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the US, repeatedly requested copies of evidence but never received most of it

The San Diego and Los Angeles FBI offices were both blocked from interviewing Bayoumi's Saudi government contacts

Staff on the 9/11 Commission objected to the conclusion that Bayoumi was "unlikely" to have been involved with extremists, prompting the report to attribute this to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him"

Omar al-Bayoumi arrived in San Diego from Saudi Arabia in 1994. He claimed to be studying English, but court records show that within a few years he had, in effect, abandoned his studies. He was more usually found organising religious events, often with a camcorder pressed to his eye.

One video Bayoumi filmed, from 1997 or early 1998, shows men, including Anwar al-Awlaki, paintballing. Filmed near San Diego, the group engages in urban combat scenes and target practice, many wearing military fatigues.

At one point, some of the men charge into battle, shouting "Allahu Akbar". A visiting Saudi sheikh is with the group and Bayoumi can also be heard addressing Anwar al-Awlaki with the honorific "Sheikh Anwar".

Paintballing emerged as a subject of interest in the FBI's post-9/11 counter-terrorism investigations, and the DOJ used paintball evidence in a number of terrorism prosecutions.

Omar al-Bayoumi and Anwar al-Awlaki were involved in paintball sessions in San Diego for at least three years in the late 1990s and very early 2000s. When the FBI investigated after 9/11, agents were told some of the participants were taking part to train for jihad.

Though Awlaki's extremist preaching would come into sharper focus after 9/11, at the time the paintballing video was recorded he already had connections to al-Qaeda operatives and was shortly to be investigated by the FBI. He was killed in a CIA drone strike in 2011.

Saudi Arabia has stated that the paintball video does not reveal who "made" or "took" it. When he was questioned remotely in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in 2021, Bayoumi insisted he had not met Awlaki. The video evidence contradicting his claim was only made available, confidentially, to the court a year later - and placed on the public docket on 4 September this year.

Another previously unreported clip shows Bayoumi embracing Awlaki in January 1998. Further footage records Bayoumi's many meetings with officials and preachers from Riyadh's Ministry of Islamic Affairs. He appears in a video with two ministry officials, one wielding a clipboard, at SeaWorld. Bayoumi passes the camera to his son and bounds into shot to record his presence with them.

The Ministry of Islamic Affairs, created in 1993, was seen as dominated by clerics who espoused a radical view of Sunni Islam and exported it around the world. It spent hundreds of millions of dollars worldwide building mosques, and sent dozens of officials to the US, some of whom oversaw a network of preachers with hard-line views.

After the 9/11 attacks, Omar al-Bayoumi emerged as an early suspect in the FBI's investigation.

His name had been found on an apartment rental agreement signed by the first two hijackers to arrive in the United States, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar, who were part of a five man hijacking team that crashed a plane into the Pentagon.

The FBI traced Bayoumi to Birmingham, UK, where he had moved with his family before 9/11.

On 21 September 2001, officers from the Met Police's Anti-Terror Branch Special Operations team arrested Bayoumi at one of his properties.

He was blue-lighted down to Paddington Green Police Station in London, where detectives began questioning him. Under UK law at the time, officers could only hold him for seven days without charge.

The following morning, in Birmingham, officers began the meticulous process of logging and bagging up evidence in his properties - a cache of many thousands of pages of documents, hundreds of photographs, flight ticket stubs, phone cards, and carrier bags and boxes containing at least 80 videotapes.

Within hours of the search starting, several items of documentary evidence - categorised as the highest priority at the direction of the FBI - were taken by police directly to Paddington Green, where the FBI had stationed an agent.

This evidence included a phone book containing more than two dozen names of Saudi government officials in the US and Saudi Arabia; flight simulator software; tickets and travel documents; and the yellow lined page of a notebook with the sketch of a plane, which an officer had marked: "contains handwritten notes mathematical calculations re height of planes".

Eighteen years later, the FBI would hand the notebook page to the court in the 9/11 families' lawsuit, following a subpoena. The page was made public in 2022.

"It's the mathematical calculation of the crash," Jodi Westbrook Flowers, a member of the 9/11 families' legal team, told the BBC. "When we figured out what it was, we knew that it was the smoking gun that we'd been looking for."

The equation, written in Omar al-Bayoumi's handwriting, indicates the height and distance required for a pilot to guide an aeroplane to a given object on the ground. Underneath it is a small drawing of a plane and a series of numbers.

Last year, the federal judge in the families' lawsuit found the notebook page, on the face of it, "connects Bayoumi with knowledge of the 9/11 Attacks".

In 2021, when questioned about it in court, Bayoumi said he had the diagram because he liked finding equations and could not remember when he had written it.

By the evening of 22 September 2001, copies of the plane diagram were in London in the hands of both the FBI and UK counter-terror police - and just metres from the custody suite where Omar al-Bayoumi was being questioned. Records show they passed through at least three further FBI agents in the following two days.

But here, the mystery begins. The FBI briefed the Met officers to question Bayoumi about the other high-priority exhibits, but the detectives in the custody suite were never given, or briefed about, the plane diagram.

Many FBI agents have told us the immediate aftermath of 9/11 was a round-the-clock frenzy. But it is hard to understand how a piece of evidence of this importance, in a case being handled with considerable urgency, was not put into the hands of the interviewing detectives.

The FBI declined to respond to our questions. The Metropolitan Police told us it could not comment because of the ongoing legal case.

Soon after the plane diagram was couriered to Paddington Green, all Bayoumi's videos, including the footage of the paintballing, were taken from Birmingham to New Scotland Yard for copying.

By 24 September, the custody suite a mile or so away at Paddington Green had access to the video cassettes. The detectives brought the bags of tapes into the room where Bayoumi was being questioned - and some of the footage was played to him.

He was asked about two tapes featuring a gathering, but the British officers were not briefed by the FBI to ask him about the video of the paintballing session - nor about his association with Anwar al-Awlaki.

On the day he would need to be charged or released, the Met detectives joined a conference call with several senior officials from the US Department of Justice and FBI.

Panorama and Radio 4 have spoken to two participants at the meeting. One recalls the British detectives setting out the evidence they believed met the threshold for the Americans to extradite Bayoumi to face charges in the US.

The response from the DOJ officials was that no extradition would be sought because there was insufficient evidence.

On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released.

But, at that point, the FBI had not shipped all of the evidence found in Birmingham back to the US, let alone exhaustively analysed it.

One memorandum from the FBI's legal attache in London, sent two weeks later, noted there were a "number of videos, floppy disks and documentation still to be viewed".

After Omar al-Bayoumi's release, agents continued analysing the evidence against him.

The BBC understands the plane diagram was couriered from London for analysis at the New York Field Office, which was in overall charge of the 9/11 investigation.

But we have not been able to trace any records of this analysis or its conclusions. A 2021 Presidential order required the FBI to declassify files relating to its 9/11 investigations, including into Bayoumi.

However, of the files released, the FBI has only produced one document referring to the diagram, despite its evidential significance, and this was only created 11 years after the diagram's initial discovery in 2001.

The diagram seems to have fallen into a black hole.

It was not passed on to San Diego, where Bayoumi had lived in the USA and where the FBI Field Office was also investigating him.

In fact, San Diego - where agents were interviewing his associates, searching his mosque, analysing his telephone records and bank statements - received almost none of the large volume of evidence seized by the Met Police in Birmingham.

Rick Lambert, who ran the FBI's investigation there, told the BBC his office made repeated requests to New York to send copies of all the evidence. "Their position was, we're in charge of the case; we'll send it to you when we're finished analysing."

Lambert said New York did not comply his office's requests. "I believe there is the potential that had we received that evidence and analysed it, that we would have been able to put the pieces of the puzzle together much more quickly."

Documents show that, in spring 2002, the San Diego office was ultimately able to get copies of a handful of videos by obtaining them not from New York, but from the FBI liaison in London.

What happened to the paintballing video is equally curious.

A copy of the tape was sent to the FBI office in New York, where it was viewed, one agent told us. But it was not included in the office's summaries documenting Bayoumi's extremist connections.

FBI and DOJ memos from 2002, viewed by the BBC, discussed materials seized from Bayoumi's homes in Birmingham that could "demonstrate Omar al-Bayoumi's anti-American sentiments and beliefs" and writings by Bayoumi himself that "can be interpreted as jihadist".

But there was no mention of the paintballing video or Bayoumi's connection to Anwar al-Awlaki.

Jeffrey Breinholt, then the deputy director of counter-terrorism at the Department of Justice who oversaw prosecutors working on terrorism charges after 9/11, told the BBC that Bayoumi's name had come up "as one of the hot possibilities for charges".

But he said the New York Attorney's Office never sent charges to him or his colleagues for approval. If they had, the plane diagram would have been significant evidence against Bayoumi, he said. "We've convicted people for less."

The paintballing video, Breinholt told us, is another "very telling bit of evidence" with the presence of Anwar al-Awlaki being "pretty damn significant".

"As a manager who reviewed a lot of proposed terrorism cases over the years, I can tell you that that would have jumped out. I think it would be a material support charge against Bayoumi."

There were no charges brought against Bayoumi.

Agents who tried to investigate Omar al-Bayoumi encountered other roadblocks.

In October 2001 in San Diego, Lambert and colleagues wanted to interview a number of Saudi officials in the US - many connected to the Ministry of Islamic Affairs - who they suspected had co-ordinated the help Bayoumi gave to two of the hijackers, Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar.

Because diplomats have a special protected status, the agents needed permission from FBI headquarters and the State Department.

"The answer came back, 'no, you're not going to do that'," Lambert, who is now a consultant for the 9/11 families in their lawsuit, told us.

Agents in Los Angeles experienced a similar outcome the following year, when they applied to interview a Saudi religious diplomat Bayoumi had met immediately after his first encounter with Hazmi and Mihdhar in the city.

"We hit a roadblock so hard, I think we all had airbag burns," said Steve Moore, who oversaw the FBI's 9/11 investigation in LA. Moore says his team made repeated requests to interview the official, but permission never came.

Like the FBI, the State Department declined to comment.

A multi-course dinner with Saudi secret police

In October 2003, the 9/11 Commission - set up by Congress to provide a "full and complete" account of the attacks - interviewed Omar al-Bayoumi in Riyadh. He had returned to Saudi Arabia in the months after his release by British police.

The interview was conducted, in the presence of Saudi secret police, by the Commission's executive director Philip Zelikow, a former advisor to President George W Bush, along with a senior staffer and an agent from FBI headquarters.

The Commission's notes from the time record that Bayoumi was given a remarkable degree of reassurance during the interview. He "was told that no-one believes he knowingly helped the hijackers carry out their terrorist mission".

Bayoumi indignantly said he was a peace-lover who had become "a victim of the victims". During the interview, the delegation broke away for a multi-course dinner hosted by the Mabahith, the secret police, without Bayoumi.

After the interview concluded, the Mabahith told the American delegation they "would like to see him cleared". The Americans responded that no exoneration would be possible before their report was published.

When the 9/11 Commission Report was published in July 2004, Bayoumi was, in effect, cleared. It described him as "obliging and gregarious" and stated there was no evidence he had extremist views.

But some staff on the Commission were not convinced of Bayoumi's innocence, and thought it likely he knew Hazmi and Mihdhar were al Qaeda operatives.

The BBC can reveal that those staff objected to a line in the report concluding that he was "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists".

In the end, a compromise was agreed, and this conclusion was attributed to "our investigators who have dealt directly with him and studied his background".

The line was written based on the four and a half hours the Commission delegation had spent with Bayoumi, which included the interruption for dinner.

The Commission never saw the plane diagram, the paintballing video, written evidence of Bayoumi's alleged extremism, or much of the rest of the evidence the Met Police had seized.

Philip Zelikow did not answer the specific questions we asked him. He told the BBC the 9/11 Commission's findings had been subject to two government reviews, in 2015 and 2021, and the Commission had been "open about our suspicions and uncertainties. We were careful about whom to accuse of complicity in mass murder."

The Department of Justice told us it was unable to comment on matters and decisions from 25 years ago, involving staff who no longer worked there.

The head of the FBI's 9/11 investigation, Mary Galligan, has previously stated the Commission had "access to everything".

We tried to contact Omar al-Bayoumi through the Saudi government, but he did not respond. He has previously denied knowing Hazmi and Mihdhar were hijackers, that he was a Saudi spy, and that he had any involvement in 9/11.

The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia did not respond to our request for comment. It has previously said any allegation that Saudi Arabia or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.

articles.title: Hot summer helps group clear bucketfuls of litter from Ellesmere
articles.summary: The hot summer has meant lakes and rivers across the country have been running low.
articles.body:
Volunteers in a north Shropshire town have been able to litter pick inside a prominent lake because its water levels have dropped due to the recent hot weather.

With this summer being the hottest and one of the driest on record, lakes and rivers across the country have been running low.

It has meant Ellesmere park ranger, Lee Fraser, has been able to go into the Mere with volunteers and pick out litter, such as bricks, pottery and mobile phones.

He said the team have already collected "five big bucket loads" of litter which he said "covered half the distance" of the town's promenade.

Fraser said this year they decided to collect litter by standing in the water, as it was easier to see what was in the water.

"We tried it last year from a boat, which when you stand on the bank, you can see all the bricks.

"Once in the water, on the boat, even if you are next to them and someone's shouting that it's right next to you, you cannot find it.

"There are quite a lot of bricks out on the side now already and we have only been at it less than an hour", he said.

He added that he thought it would take some time for the level of The Mere to recover.

"It will be quite a while [for it to recover] even with the heavy rains we have had," Fraser said.

"It is slightly deeper than it was the other week but not significantly, and over the surface of the Mere it takes quite a lot for it to get [back to normal.]

The Mere is also cared for by volunteers like local resident, Wendy Salter.

She has been part of the team for three years and said she has enjoyed volunteering to help her community.

"A lot of this rubbish comes from such a big area. [What we find] varies a lot. I also found a mobile phone last week", Salter added.

articles.title: Middlesbrough schools close early for A66 crash funeral
articles.summary: Theo Rae is one of seven killed when a car going the wrong way crashed with a Cleveland Police car.
articles.body:
A number of schools will again close early on the day of the funeral for one of the men who died in a crash which killed seven, including two police officers.

Theo Rae, 17, was among the five in a car which went the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough in the early hours of 22 August and hit an oncoming Cleveland Police vehicle.

Middlesbrough Council said some schools had chosen to close ahead of Monday's funeral, including a primary school which claimed the move would "ensure safe transit home for all our families".

Schools in neighbouring South Bank closed early on Friday for Jakub Matusiak's funeral, which police said "passed without issue" and with "very minimal traffic disruption".

Rae's funeral is to take place at Teesside Crematorium, Acklam, Middlesbrough, on Monday afternoon.

The funeral cortege is expected to travel around Middlesbrough before going to St Bede's Chapel on Acklam Road.

Cleveland Police said Ladgate Lane, Ormesby Road, Cargo Fleet Lane and Acklam Road will all be affected.

Last week, Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she trusted headteachers to make decisions to keep their communities safe.

But ahead of Monday's funeral, Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it was "obscene" to see schools close once again in the area.

"Lucy Powell should be ashamed that she has refused to intervene," she wrote on X.

Badenoch said: "It was bad enough that schools closed early last week but it is completely unfathomable that the Labour government has not stopped it happening again this week."

Labour MP for Middlesbrough South and East Cleveland Luke Myer responded by saying he was "sick of politicians like Kemi Badenoch trying to score political points when we on Teesside are dealing with a tragedy".

"She knows that since the Tories spun off our schools into academy trusts, local headteachers make decisions independently from politicians, so it's ridiculous to somehow claim it's Labour's fault."

A spokesperson for Redcar and Cleveland Borough Council said the decision last week to close some schools early came "after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport".

For Cleveland Police, Supt John Wrintmore said the closures had not been made on its recommendation but the force was liaising with others in the area about expected disruption.

He said: "There will be a proportionate visible police presence in the affected areas to ensure public safety, in line with our plans for any significant gathering."

Middlesbrough Council said some schools had chosen to close early "based on the possibility of localised traffic disruption leading to delays later in the afternoon".

Outwood Academy Acklam will close at 12:15 BST, Newham Bridge Primary School at 13:00 and Acklam Whin Primary School and Green Lane School in Acklam at 13:15.

In a letter to parents, Newham Bridge Primary said the closure was to "ensure safe transit home for all our families".

Outwood Academy Acklam said the decision had been reached "after careful consideration of the potential impact on pupils, staff and families travelling to and from the school".

The head-on crash that killed seven people on the A66 happened at 03:39 BST on 22 August.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died at the scene.

The five occupants of a VW Passat, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy, also died.

Several people have since been arrested as part of a wider police operation into organised crime.

articles.title: Bristol academic shares rags to riches story in new book
articles.summary: David Etor grew up in poverty in Nigeria, but now teaches engineering at the University of Bristol
articles.body:
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.

David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.

He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.

Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.

"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.

"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.

"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...

"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.

"She was trying to protect our integrity."

Warning issued after dead eels found in brook

Childhood pals create 'love letter' to Doctor Who

Social media inspiring new generation of bookworms

Etor's first break came whilst doing a kind of national service in Nigeria, when he realised lots of locals were being hospitalised with food poisoning, because they were trying to preserve things by drying them in fields.

To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".

"It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.

He then completed an undergraduate degree at Newcastle University and a PhD at the University of Durham, before securing his current job in Bristol.

Sir Steve Webb, the former MP and Pensions Minister, who got to know Etor through the church in Bristol, called his achievements "remarkable".

"David's message is very much that people shouldn't be defined by their upbringing or their background," he said. "They shouldn't be written off."

"I was pinching myself on my way here this morning," Etor added.

"Nothing good was supposed to come out of me."

articles.title: Brazil planted vast eucalyptus forests for pulp; 45 years later scientists found groundwater had fallen by 4.5 metres
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Brazil’s eucalyptus industry was built on a simple promise: grow trees quickly, harvest them for pulp and create a renewable supply for the global pap.
articles.body: Brazil’s eucalyptus industry was built on a simple promise: grow trees quickly, harvest them for pulp and create a renewable supply for the global paper industry. Over decades, however, the enormous plantations have transformed landscapes across parts of the country, raising concerns about what happens to water beneath the trees. In one eucalyptus-growing region of Minas Gerais, scientists found that groundwater levels had fallen by 4.5 metres over about 45 years. The discovery has added weight to concerns from rural communities that say streams have weakened and water has become harder to find. In Bahia, where vast plantations supply the pulp industry, residents have even described the landscape as a “green desert”. The story highlights a difficult environmental question: can forests planted for industry remain sustainable when they occupy huge areas and alter how rainfall moves through the landscape?How eucalyptus transformed Brazil’s landscapeBrazil has become a global powerhouse in eucalyptus production because the tree grows rapidly and provides an efficient source of fibre for pulp and paper. Vast plantations now cover parts of states including Bahia and Minas Gerais, supplying both domestic industries and international markets. The commercial appeal is clear: eucalyptus can be harvested relatively quickly and replanted, allowing companies to maintain a continuous supply of wood. But replacing diverse vegetation with enormous areas of the same fast-growing species can change the behaviour of an ecosystem. Natural forests contain many layers of vegetation, while intensively managed plantations are designed primarily for timber production. In Bahia, residents have described extensive eucalyptus plantations as a “green desert”, reflecting concerns about biodiversity, farming and water.Groundwater fell 4.5 metres over 45 yearsThe most striking evidence comes from Turmalina, in Minas Gerais, where researchers found that groundwater levels had declined by 4.5 metres over roughly 45 years. The finding is particularly significant because groundwater is a crucial reserve for people and ecosystems, especially during periods when rainfall is limited. The relationship between eucalyptus and groundwater is complex. Trees draw water from the soil and release it into the atmosphere through evapotranspiration. At the same time, rainfall that reaches the ground can either run off, be absorbed by vegetation and soil, or eventually replenish underground reserves. Large-scale changes in vegetation can therefore affect the balance between these processes. Research titled ‘Metamorphosis of the plateau: eucalyptus monoculture and land and water grabbing in Alto Jequitinhonha, Minas Gerais’ found substantial differences in groundwater recharge between eucalyptus-dominated landscapes and native vegetation. The figures do not mean every eucalyptus plantation produces the same result, but they show why long-term water monitoring matters.Farmers say rivers and water sources have changedFor communities living alongside plantations, the debate is about more than scientific measurements. Residents in Bahia have described changes to local water sources and landscapes following the expansion of eucalyptus. The Guardian reported the experience of Ercilio Souza, a founder of the Baixa Verde settlement, who recalled a local river once being sufficiently full for people to cross by canoe. Residents have connected the river's decline with the expansion of eucalyptus plantations, including those associated with Veracel Celulose. Veracel disputes the idea that its plantations simply replace natural landscapes without safeguards. The company says it follows a “mosaic management system”, combining eucalyptus plantations with protected areas, valleys, springs and native vegetation. It also says it monitors watersheds and undertakes restoration projects. The competing accounts demonstrate why the issue remains complicated: local observations, scientific measurements and corporate environmental practices all need to be considered when assessing the true impact.The bigger problem behind Brazil’s “green deserts”The eucalyptus debate extends beyond groundwater. Large monocultures can fragment habitats and reduce the variety of plants available to wildlife compared with native forests. They can also alter the way landscapes retain and distribute water. That does not make eucalyptus inherently destructive: responsibly managed plantations can provide an important renewable source of fibre and support major industries. The concern is what happens when plantations become extremely large or replace vegetation that performs different ecological functions. In Bahia, the environmental questions are closely connected to land rights and rural livelihoods. Communities have spent years contesting access to land surrounded by eucalyptus plantations. For residents, therefore, the issue is not simply whether trees are green or whether pulp is renewable. It is about whether industrial forestry can coexist with reliable water supplies, biodiversity and farming. Brazil's experience offers a wider warning: a landscape can appear greener while becoming less diverse, and potentially less capable of retaining the water communities depend upon.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kyiv air raid alerts at record high as Russia launches round the clock strikes
articles.summary: Schools, businesses and public transport are all struggling with the surge in Russian air attacks.
articles.body:
Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, according to BBC Verify analysis of government figures.

Most air attacks used to come at night but Russia's new tactic of striking Ukraine's capital during the day is causing huge disruption to schools and businesses.

The round the clock attacks have forced people to head for shelter as many as 13 times a day, with air raid alerts lasting from a few minutes to nearly four and a half hours.

Residents in Kyiv are struggling to adapt to this new reality, adding to existing stress and anxiety. The alerts force pupils to leave their classrooms and workers their offices and leave commuters struggling to get home as overland trains stop.

This has forced the government to plan a new, two-tier warning system that allows people to carry on working, travelling and studying depending on the scale of the threat.

There was a brief pause in attacks on Kyiv over the weekend while US envoys were in town for talks about trying to end the war.

But analysis of figures from the state-owned app Kyiv digital shows that since the round-the-clock Russian attacks began at the end of August, air raid sirens have sounded across Kyiv's skies on average 10 times a day.

In the seven days from Thursday 27 August, Kyiv endured 76 air raid alerts. The largest comparable number in 2022 was the week beginning 27 February when there were around 66 alerts.

Absolute comparisons are not possible because data gathered in the first few days of the invasion was sometimes incomplete. But the trend shown by the numbers is clear.

From the BBC's office, we hear the near constant rumble of air defences and drone explosions.

The more frequent Russian strikes are exacerbated by a second development, the use of newer and faster attack drones powered by jet engines. Some of these fly almost 370 mph (595 km/h), three times as fast the older Shahed drones driven by propellers, and are harder to shoot down. Ukraine's air force says Russia launched 2,800 fast drones in August, almost twice as many as in July.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has held an emergency meeting with ministers and commanders to work out how to produce new high-speed missiles that can intercept the faster Russian drones.

"You can all see that the Russians have changed the tactics of their strikes against Ukraine and, since August, have been terrorising our people, our cities and our villages far more intensely," the president said.

Diplomats say the risk is that Russia will manufacture its fast attack drones more quickly than Ukraine can develop a new generation of interceptors. Some military sources say this threat could become far greater than Russia's ballistic missiles which have largely overcome Ukraine's depleted Patriot defences.

Ukraine uses warplanes, anti-aircraft guns and shoulder-launched missiles to try to bring down the jet-powered drones.

But Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, said only about 60 percent of the drones were being shot down and they needed new interceptors to tackle the threat.

"The task now is to make them faster and equip them with specialised guidance systems so that they can shoot down jet-powered UAVs, the jet-powered Shaheds," he said.

"The key issue really is having guidance systems, because that is one of the crucial elements. It is not enough for the interceptor simply to fly fast — it has to hit the target. That is very important."

Analysts say Russia's aim is not only to weaken Kyiv's morale but also damage Ukraine's economy by targeting businesses and warehouses.

The alerts are also disrupting the start of the new academic year and forcing school children to leave their classrooms throughout the day.

When another air raid began, some students at the Drahomanov Ukrainian State University in central Kyiv headed underground; others stayed chatting on the street, such is the normality of these alerts.

Diana, a student teacher, said she did not sleep well at night and her schedule was disrupted during the day. "Sometimes it is hard because most of the day I need to go to safe places, like the metro or somewhere underground," she said. "It's a terrible time, but thank God we are alive. We go day by day."

Ihor, studying to become a chemistry teacher, said he was used to the alerts after many years of war but life was still hard. "We are annoyed by the sirens because they are constant," he said. "It destroys the quality of our education… We cannot study normally."

After a drone attack in a residential part of central Kyiv, students from a nearby school were evacuated for fear of explosions or a secondary, so-called "double-tap" attack.

Sophia, 17, told us it was very sad but this is what life was like now. "It's a little bit scary to live here in Kyiv," she said. "It's very difficult." The interview was then interrupted by another siren. "We need to go," she said. "It is very dangerous for you to stand in the streets. Maybe we can have a second detonation."

The constant air raids are a huge problem for businesses, many of which have to shut their doors every time a siren wails. We saw crowds of shop workers from Kyiv's biggest department store hanging around the streets during an alert, forced to leave their work place but not fearful enough to seek shelter.

There is also disruption to public transport. Some metro trains have to stop during an alert because they travel overground across the Dnipro river that bisects the city. This causes chaos for commuters who are forced to get on replacement buses.

To minimise this disruption, the government has agreed a new air-raid warning system with two different threat levels. A yellow warning to indicate a drone attack with less threat and fewer restrictions on work and travel. A red warning to indicate a more dangerous missile attack with more severe constraints on activity.

As ever, Ukraine is adapting to a yet another new threat. But the fear is that Russia's constant attacks now may leave the country and its capital less prepared for what many expect to be a tough winter as Russia shifts its attack back to Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Israeli airstrikes on a village in southern Lebanon kill 9 people, wound 13
articles.summary: Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town killed at least 11 people including two children and two medics, Lebanon‘s state news agency said.
articles.body: KFAR RUMMAN — Israel’s air force carried out two airstrikes early Monday on a southern Lebanese village, killing at least nine people and wounding others, including women and children, Lebanon’s Health Ministry said. Monday’s strikes came amid a new round of escalation between Israel and the militant Hezbollah group despite a truce reached more than two months ago. The strikes also came days after Israel’s military said it is in “operational control” of the strategic Ali Taher hill that overlooks several villages as well as main roads leading to the city of Nabatiyeh. The Health Ministry said one of the strikes hit a building, killing eight people including a child and two women. It added that 11 people were also wounded, including four children and two women. The ministry said that another strike on a car in the village killed a paramedic with the Lebanese Islamic Risala Scout Association and wounded two others. “We have been living in constant anxiety amid shelling on the outskirts,” said Kfar Rumman resident Fouad Chakaron as he stood in front of the destroyed building. “Now they struck the heart of the town.” Another resident, Saleh Medlej, pointed to the destroyed building and said this was home to families with children. “Are there missiles here?” he asked in reference to the building where the families lived. “I will not leave this place,” Medlej said, vowing to stay in his hometown despite the airstrikes and shelling. Earlier Monday, Israel’s military issued an evacuation warning for a home in the village of Deir al-Zahrani and shortly afterward a building was struck. There was no word on casualties. On Sunday, Israeli strikes killed at least seven people in southern Lebanon and leveled an empty hospital. A U.S.-brokered truce between Israel and Hezbollah as been repeatedly violated with Israel carrying out airstrikes in Lebanon and Hezbollah firing drones at Israeli troops. Lebanon and Israel in June signed a U.S.-mediated framework deal under which Israeli forces were to withdraw from southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah, but little progress has been made in its implementation. Hezbollah is not a party to the Lebanon-Israel talks and has said it will not give up its weapons in any area north of southern Lebanon’s Litani River. Israeli officials, meanwhile, have said they will not withdraw unless Hezbollah is disarmed throughout the country.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Satya Niketan building collapse has put MCD commissioner Sanjeev Khirwar under renewed scrutiny, with student organisations demanding his resignation over alleged civic lapses in the tragedy.Khirwar, a 1994-batch IAS officer, has been heading the Municipal Corporation of Delhi since January this year. His tenure has now come under the spotlight after a five-storey building being used as a student paying guest accommodation collapsed in Satya Niketan, killing seven people and injuring several others.The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) has demanded Khirwar's resignation, alleging that the civic administration failed to ensure the safety of students living in the area. The organisation had also protested outside the MCD office following the collapse.National Social Media Convenor of ABVP Prerna Bhardwaj said the organisation was demanding accountability and questioned the standards of student safety in the capital.The National Students' Union of India (NSUI) also staged a protest over the incident. NSUI president Vinod Jakhar alleged that the rescue operation exposed failures in disaster preparedness, equipment and management.Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta has meanwhile ordered the suspension of several MCD officials in connection with the collapse. Those suspended include the deputy commissioner, superintendent engineer, executive engineer, assistant engineer and junior engineer.The chief minister has also ordered a magisterial inquiry and said strict action would be taken against officials whose negligence or oversight contributed to the tragedy.The building, which was more than four decades old, had been operating as a student PG. CM said water had accumulated in its basement and that the combination of waterlogging and ongoing repair work had weakened the old structure.The collapse has also triggered a wider review of old and potentially unsafe buildings being used as PG accommodations, nursing homes, schools and other establishments. CM said the government was working on a policy requiring such buildings to undergo periodic structural audits and obtain safety certification.Khirwar's name earlier drew attention because of a controversy that led to his transfer out of Delhi in 2022.At the time, Khirwar, then Delhi's principal secretary (Revenue), was accused of allegedly using Thyagraj Stadium to walk his dog, with athletes and coaches claiming they were asked to leave the facility earlier than usual. articles.title: Maruti’s big festive challenge: Brezza, Victoris bookings outpace production
articles.summary: Cars News: Demand, not supply, is keeping Maruti Suzuki India Limited busy this festive season. At the sidelines of the new Baleno's launch, the company's Senior.
articles.body: Demand, not supply, is keeping Maruti Suzuki India Limited busy this festive season. At the sidelines of the new Baleno's launch, the company's Senior Executive Officer, Marketing & Sales, Partho Banerjee, spoke about Baleno demand, Brezza booking numbers and production splits, and why the industry's SUV obsession doesn't tell the whole story.New Brezza: 60,000 bookings, two-month waitBanerjee revealed the scale of demand for the new Brezza. "We have got close to 60,000 bookings now," he said, adding that this had come in "a span of 6 weeks." However, production has not been able to keep pace with demand. "We are not able to deliver 60,000 in 1 month," he explained, noting that the company has "already got a waiting of close to 2 months now." He added that all three powertrain options are performing well.Hatchbacks still matter: "There is a place for all models"Turning to the wider industry narrative that SUVs are the only segment that matters, Banerjee firmly disagreed. "Everyone said that only SUVs will rock but we always said that there is a place for all models," he said. He backed this with numbers: "Despite SUVs accounting for 57% of the overall sales, hatches and other form factors are contributing 43%... close to 2.5 to 2.7 million" units, going by an estimated industry size of 6 to 6.3 million vehicles by FY30-31.On the Baleno's continued strength, he said, "In the last 5 months we have done 80,000 plus sales. That's over 16,000 per month." He noted the model's dominance in its segment: "Today in the industry every third vehicle which we are selling in the premium hatch segment happens to be a Baleno."Balancing Brezza and Victoris productionWith demand outstripping supply for both the Brezza and the Victoris, Banerjee described how the company juggles capacity between the two. "Victoris is doing very well and we are again short of capacity there. So, now we have to calibrate between Brezza and Victoris," he said, citing last month's Brezza volumes of 18,000 units.Bookings across the Baleno, Brezza, and Victoris are outpacing what Maruti can currently build, and with festive-season buying now in full swing, the next few months will test how quickly that gap can close.

articles.title: Israel’s Katz threatens ‘full-scale war’ against PA after settler stabbed
articles.summary: The stabbing follows a wave of pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank by Israeli settlers.
articles.body:
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has threatened a “full-scale war” against the Palestinian Authority (PA) after a settler was stabbed in the occupied West Bank.

Israeli forces killed the suspect, a Palestinian man, soon after the attack, in which the 19-year-old settler was critically injured, Israeli Army Radio reported on Monday. The incident took place at an illegal settlement near the village of Usarin in the Nablus governorate.

The suspect fled the scene in a vehicle, with Israeli soldiers launching a search operation. They later said the suspect was killed after he allegedly tried to stab soldiers.

Several Palestinian villages were in lockdown after the incident, Al Jazeera correspondent Laith Jaar reported.

Israel’s Channel 12 reported that the settler suffered several stab wounds and was taken to hospital in a helicopter. His condition was said to be serious.

Reacting to the incident, Katz said, “If … the Palestinian Authority’s security mechanisms and related bodies initiate, or we know with certainty that they are about to initiate, a terror attack in the style of October 7 against [Israeli] forces and Jewish settlements — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and I have instructed the [military] to prepare for the opening of a full-scale war.”

The stabbing follows a wave of pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank by Israeli settlers.

Israeli military officials had warned that settler violence in the occupied West Bank could lead to wider unrest.

articles.title: DR BEN CARSON: The woke machine is lying in wait for a political comeback
articles.summary: Corporate America's woke machinery hasn't been dismantled — it's merely paused, and the midterm elections may determine whether Woke 2.0 returns.
articles.body: We all remember how bad it got. Just a few short years ago, it felt like every major institution — from corporate America, to media, to universities, to Hollywood, to our own government — had decided that half the population was the enemy. Speech was policed, businesses were pressured, and ordinary Americans found themselves locked out of basic services for holding the wrong opinions. A lot of people are now saying that chapter is closed. "Woke 1 was crazy," Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez said recently, laughing. Others have triumphantly declared that "woke" has been defeated. I understand the desire to move on. But those of us who lived through the mayhem shouldn’t be so quick to agree. Here’s what actually happened and why the danger hasn’t disappeared. The woke ideology that pervaded nearly every aspect of public life did not conquer American institutions by force of argument alone. Rather, it spread so rapidly because corporate America, in particular, became a willing and enthusiastic partner. GOP FRESHMAN FIREBRAND TARGETS GLOBAL CONSULTING GIANT OVER 'PLAINLY ILLEGAL' DEI PRACTICES Technology companies censored ordinary citizens for what amounted to thought crimes, major financial institutions stopped doing business with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, de-banked Donald Trump and refused to serve lawful gun manufacturers. "Green" initiatives became official policy, with nearly every major financial institution committing hundreds of billions to pursuing renewable energy and refusing to do business with coal companies and others that were on the "wrong side of history." Public displays of progressive orthodoxy became the price of admission across large swaths of the private sector. Companies understood that those then in political power were prepared to make life difficult for any entity that refused to fall in line, to say nothing of their own employees who could cause immeasurable headaches if executives strayed from the progressive worldview. What we continued to call free enterprise was, in practice, something closer to totalitarian social control administered at the corporate level. A concentrated group of technology platforms, financial institutions and cultural gatekeepers enforced a political narrative against large portions of their own user base. And rather than face a market cost for alienating half their user base, the sheer scale of these companies, and the regulatory barriers that protected them from true competition, made the costs of ideological experiments nearly invisible to those imposing them. When a handful of firms control the infrastructure of speech, payment, and distribution, market power and narrative power become one and the same. Dissent does not have to be answered — it can simply be excluded. DAN GAINOR: WE GOT TWITTER/X AS A PLATFORM 20 YEARS AGO AND GLOBAL CENSORS STILL HATE AND FEAR IT The only reason this apparatus was interrupted is that the American people changed the occupants of power. President Trump’s 2024 victory put the technology companies on notice. Several of their leaders appeared at the inauguration, some even helping underwrite the event. One major platform executive later publicly conceded that his company had made serious mistakes. But we should not be lulled into thinking these companies have learned their lesson. What we are seeing isn’t repentance, but merely temporary accommodation. The true believers remain inside these institutions: corporate boards, human-resources departments and mid-level management structures are still populated by people deeply committed to racial quotas, oppression hierarchies, green fantasies and the denial of basic biological reality. Should political power shift again, the incentive to reimpose a more aggressive and better-organized version of the same project — Woke 2.0 — will be overwhelming. THE WOKE LEFT CAPTURED THE SMITHSONIAN. AMERICA NEEDS A PATRIOT TO TAKE IT BACK This is the deeper danger. When the guts of capitalism can be ideologically weaponized, the ordinary corrective mechanisms of competition stop working. Incumbents no longer have to persuade customers or improve their products; they can simply close the gates. A free market depends on the ability of new entrants to challenge established players on the merits. A free society depends on the open contest of ideas. Both are undermined when concentrated private power decides which competitors and which viewpoints are allowed to exist. DUKE LAW'S ALLEGED RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT RULING: DOJ What ultimately checked this power was not the market itself, but the marketplace of the ballot box. The policies that followed the change in administration — ending race-based preferences in federal contracting and employment, restoring the principle of equal protection under the law and ending the use of federal funds for irreversible medical procedures on minors — restored a measure of sanity and forced corporate America to adjust its public posture accordingly. Without that governing sanity, there is little to prevent the return of the previous regime on an even larger scale. That is why the coming midterm elections matter so greatly, and voter identification is essential. Secure elections are the last reliable check ordinary citizens possess against concentrated power, whether public or private. Political leadership is not a luxury in a free society – it’s the thin line between a country in which the people still rule and one in which a handful of unaccountable institutions decide who may speak, who may bank and who may participate in public life. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION We have been given a reprieve in the current moment. The American people demonstrated that they still possess the power to correct course when they choose to use it. But, as the saying goes, eternal vigilance is the price of liberty. Institutions that spent years enforcing ideological orthodoxy have not suddenly discovered the virtues of pluralism. They have simply calculated that the political climate has temporarily changed. The moment that calculation reverses, the pressure will return – more sophisticated, more coordinated and more confident that it can succeed where it previously overreached. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The founding generation understood that freedom of thought and freedom of expression are not ornamental. They are the fundamental operating system of self-government. When those freedoms are systematically constrained by private institutions that face no meaningful competition and no democratic accountability, the fabric of society itself begins to fray. We cannot afford to treat the recent interruption of this process as a permanent victory when it is really just a pause. What we do with that pause will determine whether the next generation inherits a free country or a managed one. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DR. BEN CARSON

articles.title: 49ers broadcaster Greg Papa spent 78 days in intensive care after a bone marrow transplant; six months later his ‘impossible dream’ comeback begins
articles.summary: US News: For much of the past year, the San Francisco 49ers radio announcer Greg Papa's world revolved around hospital rooms, medical charts and the exhausting.
articles.body: For much of the past year, the San Francisco 49ers radio announcer Greg Papa's world revolved around hospital rooms, medical charts and the exhausting uncertainty of whether he would ever return to the work that had defined four decades of his life. Now, just six months after a bone marrow transplant and a series of life-threatening complications, he is preparing to step back in front of the cameras. At 63, Papa's comeback comes far earlier than doctors typically expect for patients facing a similarly complicated recovery. According to San Francisco Chronicle, Papa was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia on July 16, 2025, after the disease was discovered in his brain and spinal column. His treatment included chemotherapy and eventually an allogeneic bone marrow transplant. What followed was an exceptionally difficult recovery. Papa spent 78 days at UCSF Health, most of that time in intensive care. He developed pneumonia, both lungs collapsed, chest tubes were inserted and he spent a week on a ventilator, states the online report. Four blood clots also developed, including one that traveled to his lung. The damage to his lungs became so severe that he required supplemental oxygen simply to stand and walk short distances. At one point, even a trip to the bathroom left him struggling for breath, and he began considering whether he might eventually need a lung transplant.A recovery faster than expectedAccording to his medical team, patients undergoing Papa's type of transplant typically need 12 to 18 months to return to their pre-diagnosis level of functioning. Papa's recovery has moved considerably faster and by early September, his oxygen tanks had been removed from his home, marking a major milestone after months of relying on supplemental oxygen. He remains easily winded, however, and his lungs are still damaged. His physical rehabilitation has also become part of his daily routine. He walks roughly 2,000 steps a day, uses exercise bands and lifts light weights to rebuild strength after losing 36 pounds following the transplant. He has since regained about 17 pounds.Back where he belongsThe next milestone is returning to sports broadcasting. Papa is scheduled to appear as a studio analyst on NBC Sports Bay Area's 49ers Pregame Live before San Francisco begins its regular season against the Los Angeles Rams in Australia. He is also expected to participate in the network's postgame coverage. He has been medically cleared to potentially resume his radio responsibilities when the 49ers host the Miami Dolphins in Week 2. For a broadcaster known for meticulous preparation, returning to work means getting back to game notes, rosters, film and the detailed preparation that has characterized his career.The road ahead remains uncertainDespite the encouraging progress, Papa's doctors remain cautious. The first two years following a leukemia transplant can carry a significant risk of relapse. Patients also face the possibility of graft-versus-host disease, a potentially serious complication in which donor immune cells attack the recipient's tissues. Papa also has a history of cardiomyopathy, a hereditary heart condition diagnosed in 2023. The combination of existing heart concerns and lingering lung damage means his return to work will have to be carefully managed. Travel and high-altitude locations could present additional challenges, while even ordinary activities can leave him exhausted.An impossible comebackYet the transformation from a hospital bed to a television studio is striking. A year ago, Papa was in a UCSF hospital room undergoing chemotherapy while watching the 49ers begin their season. Now he is preparing to spend another NFL opening week talking about football. There are no guarantees about how long his recovery will last or whether he will return fully to his previous workload. But after months in which simply breathing and walking were major challenges, Papa is once again preparing game notes and planning for kickoff. His comeback is not just a return to broadcasting. articles.title: At 13, Natasha Agarwal started a school book drive; 5 years later her nonprofit donated over 250,000 books to children across the US and Africa
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2021, Natasha Agarwal was an eighth-grader with a concern that ‘too many children did not have books at home.’ Five years later, the school book dr.
articles.body: In 2021, Natasha Agarwal was an eighth-grader with a concern that ‘too many children did not have books at home.’ Five years later, the school book drive she began has grown into ‘BelieveNBooks,’ a youth-led nonprofit that has donated more than 250,000 books and reached over 50,000 children in the United States and Africa. Its growth shows how one teenager’s love of reading developed into an effort to make books more accessible to young people who need them. The organisation has expanded through volunteers, community book drives and partnerships with groups working with children and families. Along the way, Agarwal has written a children’s book and helped build a network. Her story is not about collecting books. It is about turning a passion into an organisation that keeps growing, through partnerships and by reaching one child at a time.Meet Natasha Agarwal, a teenager whose school book drive grew into an international nonprofit The idea began during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Agarwal came across news reports about children across the United States who had little or no access to books at home. The contrast with her own experience as someone who had always been surrounded by books made a lasting impression. According to ‘Points of Light,’ she began thinking about how books she had already finished reading could be passed on to children who needed them. She decided to organise a book drive at her school, initially without knowing how large the response would be.The result surprised her. Agarwal and her friends collected around 3,000 books, which were donated to the ‘Guadalupe Center’ in Florida. The success of that first effort convinced her that the project could become something bigger. That experience led Agarwal to establish ‘BelieveNBooks’ as a nonprofit. What started as a school initiative had become an organised effort to connect children with books they could read and keep.Partnerships helped BelieveNBooks reach children beyond its first communityPartnerships appear to have played a central role in the organisation’s growth. According to Forbes, Agarwal is one of two teenage nonprofit founders who built their organisations by developing relationships with people and groups that shared their missions. For BelieveNBooks, the connection with the Guadalupe Center created after that first school book drive, was an early example of this approach. The partnership helped open the door to a wider network of nonprofit collaborators.The organisation also found ways to make its work easier for volunteers to repeat. Forbes reported that simple toolkits, including outreach templates, branding materials and checklists, allowed individual ambassadors to organise book drives without having to create a new system each time. Volunteer support has been equally important. Since 2021, BelieveNBooks has coordinated with students at ‘Florida Gulf Coast University’ to help run its operations. Involving those students became particularly valuable as she continued her education while maintaining the organisation’s work in Florida.BelieveNBooks expanded from a local book drive into an international effortBelieveNBooks has steadily extended its reach since its early days. According to its website, the nonprofit has organised more than 100 book drives and now works across 28 locations, including 16 in the United States and 12 in Africa. The organisation reports that it has distributed more than 257,000 books and served over 51,000 children.Its work in Africa has also taken a different form. According to Points of Light, Agarwal wrote ‘Tales of African Women Trailblazers,’ a children’s book featuring 21 African-born women who overcame different forms of adversity. The book grew out of her research into educational inequality and her interest in giving young readers examples of what they might achieve. BelieveNBooks has worked with nonprofit partners in Ghana, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Zambia, Kenya and Uganda to distribute 10,000 copies of the book across the continent.A personal love of reading became a wider mission for NatashaBooks had been an important part of Agarwal’s own life, particularly during the pandemic. According to BelieveNBooks, reading allowed her to explore different places and ways of life even when travel was not possible. That experience shaped the organisation’s purpose. BelieveNBooks was created to provide children in need with new and gently used books, with the aim of supporting literacy, broadening horizons and helping young readers better understand the world around them.The organisation’s name also reflects that belief. According to its website, the ‘N’ in BelieveNBooks is a reference to its founder, while the wider name represents the idea that books can help children believe in what is possible. The first book drive eventually developed into a much broader network. BelieveNBooks now works through community drives, targeted book purchases and several distribution programmes designed to meet the needs of different groups of children and families.For Agarwal, the impact of BelieveNBooks is most visible when children receive books of their own and realise they can take it home and start building a personal library. The story of BelieveNBooks demonstrates how a small project can keep growing when the original purpose remains clear. For Agarwal, that purpose began with a simple belief that every child should have the opportunity to open a book and discover something new.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal holds day of mourning for more than 1,300 killed in floods
articles.summary: Nepal flags fly at half-mast to mark a day of mourning after catastrophic Himalayan floods kill more than 1,300.
articles.body:
Nepal is holding a national day of mourning to remember more than 1,300 people who died in last month’s catastrophic floods.

Government offices in Nepal and missions abroad are flying the national flag at half-mast on Monday, the 13th day since the floods, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement.

In the Hindu tradition, it is the final day of the mourning period, during which close family members stay at home and relatives visit to pay their respects. On the final day, rituals are held to pray for those who died.

The government has not planned any wider events for this day of mourning because search teams are still looking for survivors and resources are limited.

“There are no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas,” Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Center (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency.

A huge wall of mud and rock, triggered by a glacier breaking off, collapsed into a river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and China’s Tibet region on August 26, causing flooding that killed at least 1,380 people and left more than 5,500 missing.

In recent days, search teams in Nepal have rescued four people, including a Chinese national who was pulled from a tunnel at a hydropower site on Saturday. The others rescued were two hydropower workers from another tunnel on Friday, as well as a Nepali woman pulled out from her buried house on Saturday.

President Ram Chandra Paudel, the ceremonial head of state, is touring flood-hit areas on Monday and will survey damage caused by the disaster, his aide said.

In Kathmandu, family members gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the speeding up of the search for the hundreds of people who were working on hydropower projects and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekoshi River or buried by the debris.

Sumana Shrestha stood with her family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.

Her husband, a consulting geologist, was supposed to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The two-and-a-half-storey office was buried by debris.

“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. “The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.”

Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site.

He said authorities sent only a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”

Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said.

Specialised rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.

articles.title: Iran war: How US consumers spent an additional $100bn on fuel
articles.summary: The average US household has spent $763 extra on fuel in six months, as the US-Israel war on Iran pushes up fuel costs.
articles.body:
US consumers have paid an additional $100bn for petrol and diesel in the six months since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, according to a tracker from Brown University’s Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs.

Across the country, the added cost works out to roughly $763 per household, based on an estimated 131 million households nationwide.

The war on Iran has been unpopular in the United States, with a majority of Americans blaming President Donald Trump for the rise in fuel prices. Trump has dismissed concerns about rising fuel prices in an interview with Reuters news agency, saying: “If they rise, they rise.” He has instead tried to shift the blame by accusing oil companies of “price gouging”.

Trump claimed that the war would last four to five weeks, but it has entered its sixth month, with no diplomatic breakthrough in sight.

Petrol accounts for the larger share of the cost because Americans use far more of it than diesel. The price of petrol has climbed 39 percent, from about $2.98 to $4.15 a gallon ($0.79 to $1.09 per litre). Diesel has jumped even more sharply, rising more than 60 percent from $3.67 to $5.90 per gallon ($0.97 to $1.56 per litre).

Where are fuel prices highest in the US?

Fuel prices vary significantly by state. Prices are highest on the West Coast, especially in California, where high fuel taxes and carbon pricing programmes were already pushing costs up before the war even started.

According to the American Automobile Association, California has the nation’s highest average petrol price at $5.85 per gallon ($1.55 per litre), followed by Washington state ($5.51), Hawaii ($5.39), Alaska ($5.03) and Oregon ($5.01).

Indiana has the country’s lowest petrol price at an average of $3.43 per gallon ($0.91 per litre).

The map below shows a state-by-state breakdown of petrol prices. Hover over each state to see the percentage increase from before the war to now.

How higher fuel costs drive up the price of food

Oil and gas touch nearly every stage of the food chain, from fertiliser and tractor fuel on farms to refrigeration and insulation in cold storage to plastic packaging and truck fuel for transport.

As oil prices rise, these added costs accumulate at each step: production, storage, packaging and delivery.

By the time food reaches supermarket shelves, those additional costs are passed on to consumers as higher prices.

In lower-income countries, where populations spend a far greater share of their earnings on food and import large quantities of grain and fertiliser, rising oil prices could rapidly translate into food shortages.

articles.title: Greenwich and Kent 'super-university' created amid funding squeeze
articles.summary: The London and South East University Group (LASE) will be the third largest higher education institution in the UK.
articles.body:
The universities of Kent and Greenwich have merged to form the UK's first "super-university" amid sector-wide financial pressures.

The new London and South East University Group (LASE) becomes the UK's third largest, with more than 50,000 students across four campuses in south-east London and Kent.

Leaders say the institutions are "much stronger" together as higher education providers face mounting economic strain, but the University and College Union previously raised concerns that the merger signalled a "broader problem for the sector" .

The two universities, which legally merged last month, will still operate as distinct academic divisions within the group, retaining their current names.

Students will still apply to the institution they choose and degrees will be awarded in the name of Kent or Greenwich.

But the group will now be able to offer subjects that they could not before when they were separate entities, and students will be able to use libraries and access wellbeing services across the campuses in Greenwich, Medway and Canterbury.

Chief executive Prof Jane Harrington said the merger had made the universities financially stronger.

She said the combined group would also be better placed to help tackle regional youth unemployment.

"If I was to look through south-east London going out we've got areas of urban deprivation, then you go out into Medway and Kent you've got areas of rural deprivation and then we've got areas of coastal deprivation," she said.

"It's a real opportunity for us to address the very people that the government's worried about."

Harrington added: "Everyone probably now is starting to be familiar with the term Neets – basically people who are not in employment, education, or training (Neets) – and it's those very young people that we can now actually really start to look at what skills do they need."

There were an estimated 981,000 so-called Neets, aged 16 to 24, in April to June, a fall of 30,000 compared with the first quarter of the year.

The figure is still 30,000 higher than a year ago, according to the Office for National Statistics.

This is the first merger of its scale in the UK. Smaller mergers such as the amalgamation of three colleges within the University of the Highlands and Islands network have happened previously.

It comes as higher education providers in the UK have been facing increasing financial pressures, with MPs on the Education Committee warning earlier this year that there is a "real risk" a university in England could close due to insolvency for the first time.

The Office for Students, the higher education regulator in England, told the committee it feared 24 providers were at risk of becoming insolvent and closing in the 12 months from November last year, and warned 45% of higher education providers could be facing a deficit for 2025-26.

Harrington said challenges faced included additional barriers for high-fee international students, higher running costs and uncertainty in domestic student fee levels.

"So if you combine all of that, there isn't a university in this country that doesn't have to really look at their costs," she said.

LASE is writing up a lessons learned "blueprint" for the Department for Education to work as a "model" for a group structure which other universities would be able to use.

Harrington said the process was "not for the faint-hearted" but that it had been worth it.

In May, King's College London and Cranfield University, based in Bedford, announced plans to merge in August 2027.
