articles.title: Germany's AfD calls for parties to work with it after Saxony-Anhalt win
articles.summary: The far-right party is trying to form a government in the state after falling three seats short of a majority.
articles.body:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections for the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.

While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say I do not accept the vote of the people".

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was "deeply shocked" by the result, describing it as "seismic... not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously".

His party, the conservative CDU, saw its share of the vote almost halved to 17.2% in the state's preliminary results.

Merz said it was not possible to return to "business as usual", adding that the country needed "profound reforms" and the CDU needed to "reach people at an emotional level.

"This election result is a seismic result not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously," he said.

No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.

Von Storch said the state's results "were on the table and now democrats have to talk to [one] another. This is what democracy demands".

She added that if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".

Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".

The state's defeated premier, the CDU's Sven Schulze, also said the mandate to govern Saxony-Anhalt "now lies with the AfD".

Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.

The party's plans for Saxony-Anhalt, which include segregating child refugees into special classes and setting up a task-force to help detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, are highly controversial within Germany.

Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude.

"We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.

The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.

Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".

One idea being floated is whether there could be informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.

The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on migration and backs importing Russian gas.

The AfD has signalled an openness to talk with other parties but all - apart from the BSW - refuse to co-operate with the far-right.

The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.

They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally.

Commentators and political opponents called AfD's victory a watershed and break with the past.

"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters overnight. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the state's projected results on his Truth Social platform. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev then took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".

Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.

Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".

Asked about those who had expressed fears over the far-right party gaining power in the state, deputy parliamentary leader Beatrix von Storch told the BBC that its supporters were afraid of "losing our economy, they are afraid of losing our inner security".

She said conservative voters were turning to alternative political parties because they were not being listened to".

She added that the party's detractors should: "Wake up and realise what happened in several other European states... The conservative parties will disappear from the landscape as it happened in Italy, as it's about to happen in the UK, as it might also happen in France".

articles.title: World reacts to AfD victory in east Germany state election
articles.summary: French minister calls AfD’s victory a grave moment, warning of growing nationalism and its impact on European unity.
articles.body:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has won the regional election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, according to preliminary results.

AfD is set to secure 39 seats at the state parliament in Magdeburg, just short of the 42 seats needed for a majority.

The results drew a mixed response around the world, with far-right parties welcoming the news and some governments raising warnings.

Here’s how the world reacted to the news:

Lescure told RTL radio on Monday that the victory of AfD sends a “very, very worrying signal” to Europe.

He said the continent is facing “a major challenge in the face of a populist wave”, which he says is “spreading around the world today” and that “we must resist [it]”.

France’s European Affairs Minister Benjamin Haddad said the results mark “a very grave moment for Europe” and that “nationalism and xenophobia will never be the answer”.

“We cannot forget our history,” he added.

Santiago Abascal, leader of Spain’s far-right Vox party

“Congratulations, Alice Weidel and Ulrich Siegmund, on this spectacular result, which represents great hope for Germany and Europe,” Abascal wrote on X. Weidel is the AfD’s co-leader, while Siegmund is the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt.

Andr Ventura, leader of Portugal’s far-right Chega party

Andr Ventura described the result as an “historic victory”.

“Germans are also increasingly opening their eyes to illegal and uncontrolled immigration, corruption and the appropriation of our freedom and identity. Congratulations!” he wrote on X.

Poland’s Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski

Sikorski said the fact that the far-right party narrowly missed a majority was an alarming sign.

“It seems they’re just a few votes short of an absolute majority, but this is indeed a very worrying sign,” he told Radio ⁠Vox FM.

Businessman Elon Musk welcomed the results in a statement on X, simply stating “Gut gemacht!” which translates to “well done” in German.

Siegmund proceeded to personally thank Musk on X for his “support” and “clear and highly important perspective” on the “political developments of our time”.

Former Hungary Prime Minister Viktor Orban

Ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban called the win “a huge night for Germany and Europe,” and said that “this is just the beginning”.

Former US Ambassador to Germany Richard Grenell

Grenell described the victory as “a huge win and a new day for Germany”, in a statement on X. He also said that “people are ready for change”.

Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund

Dmitriev said Siegmund was the “voice of reason” in a post on X.

articles.title: Range Rover audio issue soon after delivery: Dealer, workshop told to pay Rs 1.5 lakh
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The West Bengal state consumer commission has directed a car dealer and its workshop to pay Rs 1.5 lakh to a company over poor after-sales .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The West Bengal state consumer commission has directed a car dealer and its workshop to pay Rs 1.5 lakh to a company over poor after-sales service for a Range Rover whose audio system developed problems soon after delivery. The commission, however, rejected the company's demand for replacement of the vehicle or a refund of its purchase price. The order was passed on September 3, 2026.Why did the company approach the consumer commission?According to the commission order, Zeniak Innovation India Ltd purchased a Land Rover Range Rover for Rs 53,72,177 on March 31, 2019, and the vehicle was delivered on August 5, 2019. The company said the front door did not close properly and the audio system started having problems almost immediately after delivery.The vehicle was taken to the workshop on August 19, 2019. The company said repeated checks and repairs did not solve the problems. It then sought replacement of the vehicle or a refund of its price, along with compensation and damages.Lexus Motors, the vehicle dealer, denied that the vehicle had a manufacturing defect. It said the audio complaint had been attended to and the required parts or the music system had been replaced under warranty. The company eventually took back the vehicle on November 26, 2019.What did the commission find about the Range Rover's defects?The bench comprising judicial member Rajes Guha Ray and member Santanu Sahanoted that the dealer itself had replaced the audio parts under warranty. However, it said there was not enough evidence to show that the entire Range Rover had a manufacturing defect that would justify replacing the vehicle or refunding its price.The commission also noted that Jaguar Land Rover India Ltd, the manufacturer, was not made a party to the case. It said this was important because the company had not been given an opportunity to respond to the allegation that the vehicle itself had a manufacturing defect.While the commission did not find enough evidence to order replacement of the entire vehicle, it said there was clear evidence that the audio system had a problem. It noted that the dealer itself had replaced the audio parts under warranty.“The complainant unquestionably reported an audio complaint within days of delivery. The opposite parties' admission that audio components or the system were replaced under warranty corroborates the existence of a defect in that component at the relevant time,” the commission said.The main question, therefore, was whether the dealer had properly fixed the audio problem. When the vehicle was returned to the company on November 26, 2019, the delivery record mentioned that the front-left speaker sounded different and that the sound was continuous.The commission said this showed that the audio complaint had not been clearly settled when the vehicle was returned. It observed that the dealer should have shown through proper checks that the problem had been fixed.“The delivery record of 26 November 2019, however, does not support the opposite parties' assertion of unqualified satisfaction. The feedback contemporaneously records that the front-left speaker sounded different and that the sound was continuous,” the bench further noted.The commission also looked at the sequence of events. The complaint was made within three days of delivery, the vehicle was taken to the workshop within about two weeks, and audio parts were replaced. The customer also mentioned the speaker problem again when taking back the vehicle.Based on these facts, the commission said the dealer had not properly closed the audio complaint.“The failure to close the admitted complaint with objective diagnostic confirmation constitutes a shortcoming in the manner of performance and hence deficiency in service within Section 2(1)(g) of the 1986 Act,” it held.The commission therefore rejected the company's demand for replacement of the Range Rover or refund of its price. However, it held Lexus Motors Ltd and its workshop responsible for failing to properly handle and close the audio complaint. It did not find enough evidence to uphold the company's allegation about the front door.The commission partly allowed the complaint and directed Lexus Motors Ltd and its workshop to jointly pay Rs 1 lakh as compensation for poor after-sales service and Rs 50,000 as litigation costs.It also gave the dealer one final opportunity to check and fix the audio problem. If the company presents the vehicle within 30 days of receiving the certified copy of the order, the dealer must check the audio system, particularly the front-left speaker, and fix the reported problem without charging for parts or labour. This will not apply if the problem was caused by later damage or an unauthorised alteration. The inspection and repair must be completed within 15 working days.The Rs 1.5 lakh must be paid within 45 days from the date of the order. If the amount is not paid within that period, it will carry simple interest at 9 percent per annum from the date of default until payment.

articles.title: How anti-migrant boat protests were organised and who is behind them
articles.summary: Danny Thomas organised the demonstration in Dover - seemingly after weeks of preparation - and was also present in Portsmouth.
articles.body:
This weekend saw hundreds of people take part in two anti-migrant protests. The men in balaclavas in Dover, and the crowd trying to block the migrant coaches in Portsmouth.

But how are they linked? The answer is one man - Danny Thomas, more often known as Danny Tommo - and some apparently poor decision-making by Border Force officials.

Portsmouth small boats protest 'a wake-up call for government', local police commissioner says

Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Saturday's protest in Dover saw men in black clothing and balaclavas block the town's main roads for several hours .

It was organised by Thomas - seemingly after weeks of plotting over the summer - who comes from Hayling Island near Portsmouth.

When Border Force then had to decide where to ask the RNLI to bring a boatful of migrants ashore on Sunday after an unusual longer English Channel crossing from Baie de Seine , it opted for the Eastney landing stage.

The very place where the passenger ferry departs Portsmouth for Hayling Island.

Whether this decision was made through ignorance or incompetence, it made it very easy for Thomas to mobilise his local support late on Sunday using social media.

Thomas is a long-term campaigner against migrants and says he is a Christian.

"Christ is King!" was shouted alongside "Stop the boats!" at the Dover protest.

He first came to public attention in 2016 when he was jailed for two years after pleading guilty to attempting to kidnap at knifepoint a man called Graham Page.

When he left prison, he became a close associate of the anti-migrant and anti-Muslim activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.

They appear to be less close now, though Robinson has expressed support for this weekend's protests.

Thomas has spent the last year filming himself harassing migrants on the beaches of France, and sharing the videos on social media.

In July, he announced a new venture called Patriot Platform and has been drumming up support for what he called "mass resistance", without violence.

It describes itself as a movement by "the sons and daughters of this island" designed to "take our country back".

In a video posted on Wednesday and apparently filmed with supporters in the north west of England, Thomas tells a group of men gathered on a playing field that "something is about to go down and men from all round the country will be involved in it".

"Once we pull this off it will snowball in the entire country," he says later in the clip, in which he also tells the group the movement is about "boxing clever" and exercising "discipline".

"We create a violent movement now, what do you think is gonna happen? We'll get nicked," he says.

The Dover balaclava protest, well-organised and disciplined, was the group's first outing. It is unlikely to be the last.

He seems to be borrowing ideas from groups like Just Stop Oil. Strong visual protests, with maximum disruption.

Kent Police described the protest in Dover as "spontaneous", but the force has since faced questions as to why it did not know about it in advance.

The government has meanwhile condemned the "intimidating and thuggish behaviour" of protesters in Portsmouth.

A spokesperson added: "The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder."

articles.title: Woman marks 45 years of working at Minehead Butlin's resort
articles.summary: Linda Carroll started at the resort in 1981 and says she hopes to continue there until retirement.
articles.body:
"My husband says if you cut me in half, I'd have Butlin's running through me like a stick of rock."

Linda Carroll, from Minehead in Somerset, is marking a major milestone after working at the holiday resort in the town for 45 years.

She became a permanent staff member in August 1981 and has held various job titles since. "I've met so many lovely people along the way too, many of whom have become lifelong friends from all over the country," she said.

Craig Goodwin, resort director at Butlin's Minehead, said: "Reaching 45 summers at Butlin's is an extraordinary milestone and Linda has been part of life at Minehead for generations."

Carroll added: "What I always say is where on earth can you go to work and then at the weekend come back in to sit and enjoy Fat Boy Slim?"

She first spotted her future husband, Tommy, while working at the resort in 1985, with the pair getting together the following year.

She has held various jobs including supervisor titles and management positions, before stepping into her current role helping staff across Butlin's three resorts.

Her favourite memories come from the 80s when she took part in the yearly carnivals dressed as a trapeze artist and cowgirl.

Goodwin added: "From arriving as a 20-year-old to now helping new starters begin their own Butlin's journey 45 years later, Linda has made an incredible contribution to the resort, the wider business and everyone who has had the pleasure of working alongside her."

'The man who drugged and raped me was freed from prison and went on to kill'

Childhood pals create 'love letter' to Doctor Who

Beavers filmed bonding after release in the wild

Emma Kelly worked alongside Carroll at Butlin's and said her 45 years' service was "a truly remarkable achievement and a testament to her dedication and commitment".

"She is admired not only for what she does, but for who she is, a truly lovely person inside and out," she added.

Carroll said she would remain at Butlin's for a few more years.

"I've got a couple of years until retirement but I am a bit scared to retire. I'll carry on here for as long as my mind let's me and my body."

articles.title: 'Space ecosystem has to grow': Isro chief V Narayanan defends expanding private sector role
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Isro chairman V Narayanan on Monday said the space agency remains a government organisation and dismissed concerns about its privatisation,.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Isro chairman V Narayanan on Monday said the space agency remains a government organisation and dismissed concerns about its privatisation, saying the growing involvement of private companies and startups is part of efforts to expand India’s space ecosystem.His remarks came a day after nine employee associations at Isro centres sought official clarification on the proposed transfer of some manufacturing and operational functions to private entities.Speaking to reporters after the inaugural ceremony of the ninth edition of the Bengaluru Space Expo (BSX), Narayanan said the concerns raised by employees were genuine and that it was the organisation’s responsibility to address them.“So, surely, my colleagues, whatever they have, it is a genuine concern. It is our responsibility to clarify,” he said, as quoted by news agency PTI.Asked about different voices within Isro raising concerns, Narayanan said, “We will address the employees.”Also read: Isro says its 'next chapter' is leading national space ecosystemIsro to work with private sectorNarayanan said India’s space programme was about 64-65 years old and that 56 space assets were currently operating in orbit to serve the country.He said the scale of India’s requirements meant that the number of space activities and launches would have to increase substantially.Recalling the space sector reforms introduced six years ago, Narayanan said the government’s approach was to support private companies and startups and expand the overall space ecosystem.“Since the space sector reforms were rolled out six years ago, as per that, we are supposed to hand-hold the private sector, startup companies, and grow the space ecosystem,” he said.He also said Indian industry already had a substantial role in Isro’s launch programmes.“In fact, whenever a PSLV or a GSLV is lifting off, almost 80 per cent budget is invested in Indian industries. A total of 450 industries are working for us,” Narayanan said.At the same time, he stressed that Isro itself had not been privatised.“We are working -- it's a government investment, and we are working there. But the only thing is, we now (have) so many activities. The space ecosystem in the country has to grow and the space economy has to grow,” he said.Target of 50 launches a yearNarayanan said India’s requirements would eventually require around 50 launch vehicles a year.“The country's requirement is around 50 launch vehicles per year. We have to go ahead,” he said.He recalled that when he joined Isro 43 years ago, the organisation conducted one launch roughly once every three years.“So many activities are going on. Probably one or two things are only known outside, but it is our responsibility to put everything in the Isro side. Fifty launches per year is going to be a reality,” he said.Narayanan added that the target would be achieved “by Indians in India”.The target of 50 launches a year by 2030 has also been cited by IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka, who said the scale would require government and private industry to work together.Also read: Isro will never be privatised, its role won't be diminished - Space Agency & INSPACe chiefEmployee associations seek clarityThe nine employee associations had written to Narayanan on September 4 seeking clarification over the direction and basis of the transition towards greater private-sector participation.The associations represent employees at several Isro centres and raised questions over whether launch-vehicle design, development, integration, testing and launch operations would continue as Isro functions or be transferred to private entities.Also read: In a first, 9 Isro staff bodies seek 'written clarity' on private sector shiftThey also sought clarity on the future role of public-sector units, the transfer or opening of publicly developed technology and infrastructure to private operators, and the respective roles of NSIL and IN-SPACe.The employee bodies expressed concern that a progressive withdrawal of Isro from launch-vehicle and satellite realisation could affect in-house work, recruitment, sanctioned posts and career opportunities.Isro had said on Sunday that suggestions that the agency would be privatised or its importance reduced were “completely baseless and incorrect”.The agency said it would continue as India’s principal institution for advanced space research and technology development, national and strategic missions, space science and exploration, and critical and frontier space capabilities.It also said greater private-sector participation was intended to allow industry to scale mature technologies while Isro focused more on areas including frontier research, advanced technologies, human spaceflight, next-generation launch systems, deep-space and planetary missions, and strategic capabilities.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Could Trump’s Iran trade war threaten Spain’s saffron-infused paella?
articles.summary: US threats to punish Iran’s trade partners could disrupt Spain’s saffron supply, pressuring paella chefs and exporters.
articles.body:
Madrid, Spain – Fields of purple flowers contain crimson stigmas that make saffron, an essential spice in Spain’s national dish, paella.

Saffron gives the rice-based dish its distinctive yellow colour and earthy aroma.

Though the central Spanish region of Castilla-La Mancha grows its own crop, Spain depends largely on Iran for its supply.

This could now be under threat after the United States said in late August that it would launch an “economic onslaught” against Tehran’s trade partners around the globe to cripple Iran financially. The United Arab Emirates also said it would suspend trade relations with Iran.

Exactly how Washington would take measures against all of Iran’s trade partners remains unclear, although on September 4 the US Treasury Department announced sanctions on Turkiye’s Golden Global Bank, which the US accuses of facilitating funds for Iran, CNBC reported.

“This threat from the United States could be a problem for us. Our biggest supplier by far is Iran. Then we sell it to markets all over the world,” Jose Luis Guerrero, of CEAE, a Spanish saffron export company that began in 1904, told Al Jazeera. “We will have to worry about it when the US says what action it will actually take.”

Maria Naranjo, director for agrifoods at ICEX, Spain’s state trade and investment body, said Spain was a “particularly important” gateway of saffron into Europe. Two years ago, Spain accounted for three-quarters of EU imports of saffron from Iran.

“This highlights the role played by Spanish companies not only as importers but also in processing, packaging, branding and distributing saffron to international markets,” she told Al Jazeera.

“Against this background, any potential disruption to trade flows with Iran would not necessarily result in a shortage of saffron for Spanish consumers or for its use in Spanish cuisine. The impact could be more significant for Spanish companies involved in importing, processing, packaging and internationally distributing the product.”

Until the full details of US sanctions are known, it will not be possible to work out the impact on the Spanish saffron trade, Naranjo said.

“We still have saffron from Castilla-La Mancha. Paella is not in danger,” she joked.

Analysts say the success of the US strategy largely depends on China, the main buyer of Iranian oil and its leading trading partner.

“Those who stand with the United States will reap the rewards of our partnership,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said. “Those who tether themselves to the Iranian regime should expect to share in the isolation.”

Washington’s threats against Iran’s trading partners have sent alarm bells ringing.

Spain’s commercial links with Iran are minor compared with countries like Turkiye and Pakistan.

In 2025, Spanish companies exported products worth $143m to Iran and imported Iranian goods worth $141m – a total of almost 245 million euros ($285m) in the bilateral trade of goods, according to Spanish government figures.

Imports of saffron were worth $61m, more than 40 percent of all imports from Iran.

US-Spain relations, meanwhile, have been strained .

President Donald Trump and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez have previously clashed over defence spending among NATO member states.

In July, Trump threatened to cut off trade relations with Spain, saying Madrid had been a “terrible partner in NATO”.

However, the threat was not followed through.

The US and Spain have also been at odds over Sanchez’s condemnation of the US-Israel war on Iran , which he said was “illegal”.

And while the Spanish prime minister condemned Hamas’s attack on southern Israel in 2023, he has also criticised Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

But Vicente Roja, a paella chef from Valencia, the home of Spain’s signature dish, is unfazed.

“No one can touch our paella. It is the essence of Spain. Whatever happens, we will get by.”

Spanish people are famously proud of paella, and new takes in the past been followed by light-hearted rebukes.

In 2022, the British supermarket Tesco touched a nerve when it dreamed up a paella sandwich. In response, Spain’s Civil Guard, which is normally busy catching criminals, marked World Paella Day.

“The paella sandwich for some is heresy, for others it slaughters good taste and could even threaten health,” it said on social media, with smiley emojis.

In 2016, Jamie Oliver, the British television chef, committed a similar gastronomic offence when he suggested adding chorizo to the dish. The seemingly harmless suggestion prompted claims that he was a “culinary terrorist”.

articles.title: Discovery beneath soccer field reveals massive medieval convent lost for centuries
articles.summary: Ground-penetrating radar revealed St. Clare's Convent buried three feet under a Danish soccer field, stunning archaeologist Jesper Langkilde, who shared insight with Fox News Digital.
articles.body: Researchers recently uncovered a long-lost medieval convent in an unusual location in Denmark: a soccer field — with an expert sharing details with Fox News Digital about the "rare" find. The discovery, made in Roskilde, was announced last month by ROMU, a state-recognized Danish museum organization. St. Clare's Convent, which was built in the 13th century, was found through a ground-penetrating radar survey ahead of plans to build an underground parking facility. FORBIDDEN PASSAGE? SECRET MEDIEVAL TUNNEL FOUND BENEATH ANCIENT PAGAN GRAVES, ARCHAEOLOGISTS SAY "The survey revealed a well-preserved convent complex approximately one meter [three feet] below ground level," officials said in a press release. The scans also "revealed traces of the convent’s buildings, including rooms, columns, cloisters and a church in the southern wing," officials said. "The eastern wing, in particular, is exceptionally well-preserved, with clearly defined rooms and vault pillars," the statement said. St. Clare's was one of five monastic sites in medieval Roskilde. Unlike the other four, it was not protected as an ancient monument because it was believed to have been lost. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH REMNANTS OF FORGOTTEN CITY 'MARKED BY CONFLICT' BURIED BELOW BUSTLING HUB Researchers are working with the municipality on plans for trial excavations at the proposed parking site. Excavations of monasteries and convents are "rare," said Jesper Langkilde, an archaeologist and museum curator at ROMU. Langkilde told Fox News Digital he was "quite surprised" by the discovery. "I almost didn’t believe my own eyes that so much was still there, and that we got such a clear image of it," he said. The convent was a large complex, measuring roughly 230 feet by 230 feet. Although the convent was demolished in the 16th century and hundreds of thousands of its bricks were removed, much of its underground footprint survived. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER LOST MEDIEVAL CITY THAT VANISHED WITHOUT A TRACE: 'TRUE TIME CAPSULE' Langkilde said the radar is detecting the lowest portions of the walls and foundations, which were made with large boulders that were often left in place when medieval buildings were torn down. Historical records show that about 500,000 bricks were sold after the convent was demolished, but Langkilde said a complex of its size could easily have contained twice that number. Though there hasn't been an excavation of the site yet, Langkilde said archaeologists expect to find "quite a lot of artifacts," especially those from daily medieval life. Excavators expect to find everything from "lots of pottery sherds and animal bones" to "religious objects, like pendant crosses, rosary beads and pilgrims' badges" and objects related to writing and books, he said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "The convents and monasteries were centers of literacy and had libraries and book production," added Langkilde, noting that book fittings, writing utensils and personal effects like combs and needles are also expected. If organic remains are well-preserved, archaeologists could learn more about the nuns' diets and the plants grown in the convent gardens. "[The discovery] is very significant, since we know very little of the monasteries in Roskilde from an archeological point of view." Researchers also expect to find burials at the site, which "can tell us about who the nuns were and who else was buried at the convent," Langkilde said. The discoveries could also reveal the convent's international connections. Its first nuns are believed to have come from a convent in Strasbourg, according to Langkilde. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "The convents were part of international networks, so it would be interesting to look for signs of international relations in the [material] from this site," he said. "[The discovery] is very significant, since we know very little of the monasteries in Roskilde from an archaeological point of view," he said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The expert also called the discovery "a very big step forward for our knowledge of the medieval monasteries." "[They] played a key part in the development of Roskilde as one of the most important and wealthiest towns in medieval Denmark," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Langkilde added, "It is an excellent example of how much archeological knowledge a geophysical survey can contribute — under the right circumstances — without even putting a shovel to the ground."

articles.title: Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital
articles.summary: Hafidh Ameir Hassan kept a low profile and was rarely seen in public with the president.
articles.body:
The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar.

Vice-president Deogratius Ndejembi - who made the official announcement of Ameir's death - said he had been suffering from a heart condition.

Ndejembi added that funeral arrangements are under way in Kizimkazi, a village on the country's semi-autonomous island of Zanzibar.

Ameir was an agricultural academic who largely kept a low public profile. He became Tanzania's first First Gentleman after President Samia took office in 2021.

In his announcement, Ndejembi said Ameir died at 08:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on Monday at the Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital.

The vice-president led tributes as he conveyed his condolences to Samia, as well as Ameir's family and friends.

Kenyan President William Ruto said he received the news of his passing with "deep sorrow".

"President Samia has lost a lifelong companion, her children a beloved father, and Tanzania a distinguished son," he wrote on social media.

Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema also shared his condolences, saying that they "stand side by side" with the first family, and all of Tanzania during "this difficult time".

Similarly, Burundi's President Évariste Ndayishimiye paid his respects and prayed for Samia and her family to have "comfort and strength in this difficult moment".

"May he [God] grant eternal rest to the soul of Hafidh Ameir Hassan," he added.

The First Gentleman rarely appeared in public alongside the president. He was only occasionally seen with her at official events.

He married Samia in 1978, before she entered national politics. The couple had four children - three sons and a daughter - together.

Their daughter, Wanu Hafidh Ameir, is also a politician who currently serves in Zanzibar's House of Representatives in the National Assembly.
